segments.text: Mr. Beast. I bet you never thought you'd see this guy in a marketing course, but if you think about
it, he gets tens, hundreds of millions of people to watch his videos from start to finish on every
single video he makes. And if that's not mastery of attention, I don't know what is. Now, obviously,
we're not making 30-minute YouTube videos here, but the principles this guy uses to keep people
watching pure fucking gold for ads. Because whether you've got three seconds or three minutes or 30
minutes, the psychology of holding attention stays the same. So across billions of views that Mr. Beast
team generates on YouTube, they saw the same patterns over and over. And in this video, we're
going to break some of them, explain how they work, why they do so well, why they retain people so well
in a video. And I'll try to explain how to apply those for our ads. Here's something fascinating
about how human brain works. So we are hardwired to pay attention to things that create open loops
in our mind. For example, imagine someone starts telling you a story and it's very interesting,
you're very invested, you're listening to them, and then someone calls them and they get interrupted.
And you're just sitting there and your brain is itching to know how the story ends. Well,
Mr. Beast team are fucking masters at this. For example, take their video of I spent 50 hours buried
alive. They open a loop in the first few seconds. Will he survive 50 hours buried alive? That's the
main hook. But then they layer it. Oh shit, like there's a storm coming and coffin might flood. And then
his oxygen levels are dropping. What's going to happen next? The support team is considering pulling
him out. Like each new problem creates another loop that your brain needs to see closed. In ads,
we do the exact same thing just faster. For example, let's say you're selling a weight loss supplement
and let's layer some loops. First loop, we show someone who lost 50 pounds and that instantly opens the
how did they do it question in viewers mind. Second loop, we show them demolishing a box of pizza while
being skinny or fit. And that creates that weight. They can eat that and still look like that question
in your viewers mind. And then we add the third loop. We show the before and after photo. And the before
photo is actually from just 90 days ago. And now the viewer's brain is scrambling to understand
how such a dramatic change happened so fast. And they're still enjoying pizza, all these tasty
foods. Fourth loop, we show testimonials of others getting the same results. And that opens the question,
so this works for everyone and not just this one person. And they see what we did there. Each new
reveal, each new kind of part of the structure doesn't just add information, it completely shatters
what the viewer thought was possible. Their brain is now racing, how can someone lose that much weight
while eating whatever they want in just 90 days, and it works for everyone. Now they're itching to know
how they did it. And notice how we haven't revealed our product yet. We're intentionally building tension,
stacking these results that seem impossible, making people emotionally invested before we even show them
the solution. Think about what happens when people see ads. The moment someone sees your product too early
in an ad, their brain goes into skeptic mode. Oh, it's just another supplement. Oh, it's just another
scammy weight loss program or something like that. But when you build these loop first, when you make
them question everything they they thought they knew about weight loss. Now they're not just watching
your ad, they're emotionally invested in finding out how this is possible. They're probably thinking
stuff like no way this works. And obviously, they are probably still skeptic about the whole thing as they
are with other ads. But now they're also thinking, what if this is that one thing I've been missing?
What if this actually works for all of those people? And they're getting hopeful, they're getting hope
that this could actually solve their problem. That's the power of these loops. By the time you reveal your
product, they're not just watching, they're waiting for the answer. And that's exactly when they're most ready
to hear about your product. But creating open loops is just one part of the equation. Now let's talk about
how to actually edit like Mr. Beast. So the worst thing you can do when editing ads is to start with a
strong hook, you know, starting with dynamic and fast paced editing, showing a bunch of clips or whatever,
but then just fizzle out the energy drops, the pacing gets weird. And you honestly half ass the rest of the
ad. And that's what happens when editors only focus on hooks and forget about everything else.
Your viewers aren't stupid. They can tell when you put all your effort into the first three seconds and
then just half ass the rest. And the moment they sense that their trust is gone, and they're gone.
They're not invested in the ad anymore. And that's why Mr. Beast's team is so obsessive about every single
second of their videos, and why we need to be just as obsessive about every frame of our ads.
Which brings us to editing principle number one, visual variety and pacing. So Mr. Beast mastered
something crucial. He never lets your eyes get comfortable. If you watch any of his videos,
you'll notice that every three to five seconds, there's a new camera angle. Every 10 seconds,
there's a new scene or a new development. Every 20-30 seconds, there's a new mini story or a
challenge development. But it's not just random changes. Each visual switch serves a purpose.
For example, he uses close-ups of people for emotional moments. He uses wide shots for scale
and impact. You know, when he does like a huge zoom out and you see like the whole area where there are
something like that. He then shows reaction shots for authenticity, just raw camera footage, like behind
the scenes stuff. And his team knows exactly when to speed or slow down. Now for ads, we need to take
this principle and compress it. We don't have minutes, we have seconds. And what's crucial to understand is
something needs to happen every two to three seconds of your ad. I would even say every one second in your
ad, something needs to happen. Either a B-roll has to change or a new animation, new text has to come up.
Something has to change. Because as you know, people are scrolling at light speed through their feed.
And if your ad doesn't keep giving them new visual information every couple of seconds, like I said,
a new angle, a new product shot, some text popping up, they're gone. But this isn't a one-size-fits-all
rule. You need to match your editing to your audience. If you're targeting Gen Z, for example,
yeah, you might need something happening every single second. You might need, you know, quick edits,
brain rot editing, however you, however you want to call it. But if you're making a ad for people in
their sixties, making it fast and hectic would be probably the worst thing you can do because
they, they can't keep track of all of that. So again, the key is understanding your audience and
understanding who the video is for, and then matching the editing and matching the style to look
like the content they already consume every day. Principle number two, progress bar psychology.
So this is a thing Mr. Beast does, especially in his sponsor segments of his videos. He uses this
psychological trick with progress bar. That's absolutely genius. And watch what he does. He
starts with the progress bar that moves super quickly at first. Within the first 10 seconds,
it's already at 50%. Like the bar is halfway there. And your brain sees that and thinks,
oh, this is going to be quick. And like, let me give it a watch, but then it slows down. Like the
second half takes way longer. But the thing is you're already invested. You've watched half of it.
So now your brain thinks, well, I might as well finish it now. And we can use this exact same psychology
in our ads. For example, we may have a hook talking about how a skincare product gives you results in just
two weeks. And instead of just jumping straight into before and after, you maybe start talking about
something else and put a little timer somewhere saying, see results in 15 seconds. And the timer
starts. And now your viewer has a clear expectation. They know exactly how long they need to pay attention
for before they get rewarded for watching the video. Or let's say you're showing customer testimonials.
Instead of just throwing them back to back, add a small progress bar that fills up with each one.
This could also be a killer technique as well for when doing VSLs, for example, where you're really
diving into the problem from the start of the ad. And maybe you spend that first part of the ad really
digging into problem, their pain points, struggles. And then here and there, you maybe mention this
breakthrough solution you found, but you never really reveal exactly what it is. You never really
reveal your product until later in the ad. And then right before you reveal your product,
that's when you hit them with revolutionary solution revealed in 20 seconds. And then you start the timer.
And while that timer is coming down, you're reinforcing everything you've talked about.
And by the time that timer hits zero, they're at the edge of their seat waiting to see what the
solution is waiting to see your product. So the whole point of this progress bar technique,
whatever you want to call it, is people will stick around more when they know exactly how much
longer they need to pay attention for. They're way more likely to watch the video or part of the video
until the end, because they can see they're actually making progress and that rewards them as they're
watching. And that's how you utilize progress bars in your ads to boost retention. So let's sum up what
we have learned from MrBeast and how we can apply that to our ads. First, we have open loops, where we
make people need to know what happens next by stacking reveal after reveal. And each one is more intriguing
than the last. Second, and I would say this one is the most important one from this video,
that's visual variety and never letting your viewers eyes get comfortable, but always matching
your editing pace to your audience. And third, progress psychology, using visual cues and timers or
progress bars, whatever you want to call them, to keep people invested until the end and give them some
kind of rewards for completing parts of your video or completing the whole video until the end. And
before we move on, I've put together a type file below this video with some amazing examples of ads and
organic videos that use some of these principles. So you can take inspiration when working on your own
ads. And at the end, remember a scroll stopping hook might get people to pause, but it's these retention
principles that keep them watching to your ad. And in a world where attention is the most valuable currency,
that's how you win.
